Correctly the Byzantine scholiast says δύσβατόν [hard to tread] of Persia, not as hard and difficult for entry, but as trodden by Xerxes for evil and misfortune. In most copies it is δύσβακτος, in one δυσβάϊκτος, from which Brunck made δυσβάϋκτος.

in M by a second hand is written above δυσευνήτειρα [hostile to the bed], which passed into many copies. The scholiast read the plural, although not δράκοντας [serpents], but seems to have read δράκοντα δ' [but a serpent]. For he writes thus: δυσευνήτορας δὲ δυσευνήτους διὰ τὸν φόβον τοῦ δράκοντος [hostile to the bed, i.e., making the bed hostile, because of fear of the serpent].
serpents (thus Both for δράκοντα δ᾽ [but a serpent]) as someone fears for his children, hostile to the marriage bed (thus Blomfield for δυσευνήτορας).
